1:
The chapter opens with the whole people of Judah setting the sixteen-year-old Uzziah upon his father Amaziah's throne, and the witnesses read the accession as the threshold of a reign that will run brilliantly and then break. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sketches the arc in advance: the people, he says, all agreed to place this son upon his father's throne, and the young king would begin his reign piously and prosperously — subduing the Philistines, the Arabians and the Ammonites, fortifying Jerusalem, delighting in husbandry, and marshalling a great army — until, elated by success, he would invade the priest's office and be smitten with leprosy, forced at last to abdicate to his son Jotham. The reformed John Gill notes only that this is the king called Azariah elsewhere, and passes the reader on to the parallel record at 2 Kings 14:21.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes that double name his study. The chronicler, he observes, calls him Uzziah everywhere save one place, 1 Chronicles 3:12, where Azariah stands, as it does in the Kings account at 2 Kings 15:1; yet Uzziah too occurs in Kings and in the headings of the prophecies of Hosea, Amos and Isaiah. It is not, therefore, to be judged a popular abbreviation or a transcriber's blunder, as Schrader and others suggested; for in the Assyrian inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser this king is uniformly called Azriyahu, that is, Azariah. Clearly, Ellicott concludes, he was known by both names, but to foreigners chiefly by the latter.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the moral frame for all that follows. Uzziah's piety, he grants, was neither very eminent nor zealous, yet he did that which was right in the sight of the Lord: he kept up the pure worship of the true God as his father had done, and was in one respect better than his father, for we have no reason to think he ever worshipped idols — not even in his latter days, when his heart was lifted up. Henry ties the whole prosperity of the reign to this one root: as long as Uzziah sought the Lord and minded religion, God made him to prosper; for those only prosper whom God makes to prosper, prosperity being his gift, and religion and piety being very friendly to outward prosperity. The witnesses do not divide. Clarke charts the reign's rise and ruin, Gill and Ellicott fix the man behind the two names, and Henry names the principle — a throne that stands or falls with its seeking of God — which the chapter will prove first in Uzziah's greatness and then in his fall.
5:
"He sought God in the days of Zechariah" — and the witnesses gather around the shadowy counsellor whose life marks the boundary of Uzziah's faithfulness. The reformed John Gill first clears away the false identifications: this is not the Zechariah who was last of the prophets but one, who lived three hundred years after; nor the Zechariah whom Uzziah's grandfather Joash had slain; but, as it may seem, a son of that murdered priest. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confesses we know this man only by the character given him here — one wise in the visions of God, skilled in interpreting the divine oracles, and probably, Clarke judges, the tutor of the young king.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the verse a study in text and idiom. "He sought God" is, more exactly, "he continued to seek God," an expression peculiar to the chronicler; and the phrase rendered "had understanding in the visions of God" is literally "the skilled in seeing God," a surprising epithet found nowhere else. Here Ellicott parts from Gill and Clarke: several Hebrew manuscripts, together with the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic and Targum, read not "in the visions of God" but "in the fear of God" — a reading he judges doubtless correct, so that the clause should run, "who gave instruction in the fear of God," the very sense that the great rabbis Rashi and Kimchi long since proposed. Zechariah was thus the guide and counsellor of the king, and that not only in religion but in what we should call the political sphere, for in those days the distinction between things sacred and secular was wholly unknown.

Ellicott adds the pointed observation that where the chronicler grounds Uzziah's prosperity in his seeking of God, the parallel at 2 Kings 15:4 makes only the usual deduction, that the high places were not taken away. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the abiding lesson from the phrase "in the days of Zechariah." Happy, he says, are the great men who have such counsellors about them and are willing to be advised by them; but unhappy those who seek God only while they have such helpers at hand, and have not a principle in themselves to bear them out to the end. The very wording, Henry warns, hints at the tragedy to come: Uzziah's devotion was propped upon another man's, and when that prop was gone his heart would be lifted up to his ruin. The witnesses converge on a portrait of borrowed piety — real while it lasted, God-rewarded while it lasted, but resting on a counsellor rather than on a settled heart.
6:
With Elath secured, Uzziah takes the offensive, and the witnesses trace his war against the Philistines both as history and as the reversal of an old humiliation. The reformed John Gill recalls that these were the very Philistines who, in the days of Jehoram, had broken in upon Judah and distressed her, as recorded at 2 Chronicles 21:16; now the tables are turned. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the campaign in order: Uzziah took the field to chastise the Philistines and Arabians who had under Joram plundered Jerusalem, broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod — that is, after capturing those cities — and built cities of his own in their territory, whence we gather that he had wholly subdued Philistia. Gath, they note, David had already taken, as at 1 Chronicles 18:1; Jabneh, here named for the first time, is the Jamnia of the Maccabees and Josephus, now the village of Jebnah south of Joppa, and probably the Jabneel of Joshua 15:11.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms and enlarges the account. At the outset of his reign, he says, this able prince had given promise of his future by seizing and fortifying Elath, thus completing the subjugation of Edom his father had begun; afterwards he assumed the offensive against the Philistines, Arabs and Maonites who had invaded the land under his predecessors, as at 2 Chronicles 20:1. Ashdod he identifies with the modern Esdud, one of the five sovereign Philistine states, commanding the great road to Egypt — hence its possession was of first-rate importance to the contending powers of Egypt and Assyria, and Sargon would capture it in 719, as Isaiah 20:1 attests. Uzziah, Ellicott judges, reduced the Philistines to complete vassalage, yet did not annex them: they were still ruled by their own kings.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill marks the poetic justice of a subdued Philistia; Keil and Ellicott fix the cities, their sites and their strategic weight, and read the whole war as the flowering of the promise made in the rebuilding of Elath. Behind the military detail all three hear the note the next verse will make explicit — that these conquests were not the mere prowess of a strong young king but the gift of a God who, while Uzziah sought him, made him to prosper. The nation that under a faithless Jehoram had been broken into and pillaged is, under a seeking Uzziah, carrying the war back into the enemy's own country and planting Judah's cities where the Philistine strongholds had stood.
7:
"And God helped him" — the witnesses fasten on that phrase as the true secret of every victory the chapter records. The reformed John Gill will not let the reader miss it: Uzziah did not do all that has been related of himself, nor by his own strength, but by the help of God; and he notes the Targum's reverent expansion, "the Word of the Lord helped him." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke cites the same Targum, that the Word of the Lord helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabians who dwelt in Gerar and the plains of Meun — peoples he takes to be the Arabs elsewhere called Meunim or Meonites.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the help across three enemies at once: as against the Philistines, so against the Arabians who dwelt in Gur-baal and against the Maanites, God gave Uzziah the victory and made them tributary. Gur-baal, they observe, occurs only here and its position is unknown; the Targum supposes the city Gerar to be meant, while the Septuagint, thinking of the Edomite capital, renders it "upon Petra." The Mehunim they identify as the inhabitants of Maan. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees, noting that Philistines and Arabians are coupled as Judah's enemies at 2 Chronicles 17:11 as well; that Gur-Baal, mentioned only here, is unknown, whether Gerar or Petra or the proposed Gedor-Baal; and that the Mehunim are the Maonites, the people of Maon near Mount Seir, whom he had already met at 2 Chronicles 20:1.

The witnesses do not divide, and they leave the obscure place-names as obscure as they found them — honest that Gur-baal cannot be located, content to let the versions guess between Gerar and Petra. What none of them will surrender is the theology stamped on the verse. The strong towers and the great army that the following verses will catalogue are real, but they are not the ground of the triumph; the ground is that God helped him. Gill's insistence, echoed in the Targum's "Word of the Lord," is the very point the chapter is building toward its terrible reversal: the same king who is helped so long as he leans on God will, when his heart is lifted up, discover what it is to be resisted by the God who once helped. Here, at the height of his rising power, every subdued Arabian and every tributary tribe is quietly credited not to Uzziah's sword but to heaven's aid.
8:
"And the Ammonites gave gifts to Uzziah" — and the witnesses agree that the "gifts" are the tribute of a subject people, not the offering of friends. The reformed John Gill takes them as tributaries, or at least as neighbours desirous to live at peace with so formidable a king. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says flatly that they paid an annual tribute. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott names them the old enemies of Judah, met before at 2 Chronicles 20:1, and renders "gave gifts" as "paid a present or offering" — the Hebrew minchah, the standing word for the tribute a weaker state renders to a stronger.

On the fame that followed, the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the phrase carefully. Uzziah's name, the text says, spread abroad even to the entering in of Egypt; and this means, in the connection, not merely that his renown travelled so far, but that the report of his victorious power reached the very frontiers of Egypt, for he had extended his rule to near that border. The clause "for he strengthened himself exceedingly" Keil glosses by the verb that denotes showing or exerting power, the same used at Daniel 11:7. Ellicott hears in the reach of that name an echo of Solomon's own greatness, whose influence had likewise touched the Egyptian border; "he strengthened himself" he renders "he showed strength, prevailed, made head," and records the Syriac's blunt paraphrase, "because he made much war." For that idiom of a king exceedingly magnified Ellicott points to his notes at 1 Chronicles 29:25, where the LORD magnified Solomon in the sight of all Israel.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott fix the Ammonite tribute as the badge of vassalage; Keil and Ellicott measure the fame that ran to the borders of Egypt and read it as the fame of real power, not of empty rumour — the report, that is, of a dominion actually pushed to the frontier, not a mere traveller's tale. Yet even here, at the summit of the king's expanding dominion, the seed of danger is quietly sown in the closing words the witnesses expound — "he strengthened himself exceedingly." It is the very phrase that the sixteenth verse will pick up and turn against him: "when he was strong, his heart was lifted up." The strength that here spreads his name to Egypt is the strength that will presently tempt him into the temple, and the self-strengthening that is now his glory will become, unbalanced by gratitude, the beginning of his fall. For now, though, the verse stands as pure ascent: a king made tributary of his neighbours, his name carried to the Nile, his power exceedingly established under the God who was helping him.
9:
The king who carried the war abroad did not neglect the defence of his capital, and the witnesses follow his builder's eye along the walls of Jerusalem. The reformed John Gill fixes on the corner gate, which had been broken down in his father's time — a breach he not only repaired but strengthened by raising a tower upon it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the whole verse as a measured programme of fortification: in order to establish the power of his kingdom enduringly, Uzziah built towers at the gates and strengthened the wall of the citadel. The corner gate they place at the north-west angle of the city, treated already at 2 Chronicles 25:23 and 2 Kings 14:13, and the valley gate on the west side, where the Jaffa gate now stands — the two quarters from which Jerusalem was most open to attack.

The "turning of the wall" Keil and Delitzsch locate, from Nehemiah 3:19 and following, on the east side of Zion, at the point where the wall crossed over at an angle to the Ophel and joined the south wall of the temple hill, so that the tower there defended both Zion and the temple against assault from the valley to the south-east. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees at every point: the towers were raised to defend the approaches; the corner gate commanded the north-west; the valley gate, which the Syriac calls simply "the west gate," guarded the modern Jaffa quarter; and the tower over the angle protected both Zion and Moriah against attacks from the south-east. The closing words "and fortified them" both witnesses take of the strengthening of the towers, putting them in a posture of defence, and Ellicott notes that the margin's rendering is wrong.

The witnesses do not divide; theirs is a shared piece of topography, tracing the same three strong points around the vulnerable sides of the city. Yet the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds the reflection that lifts the masonry into moral significance. Much of the wall of Jerusalem, he recalls, had been broken down in his father's time, particularly at the corner gate; but Uzziah's best fortification of the city, Henry insists, was not his towers at all, but his close adherence to the worship of God — for had his father not forsaken that worship, the wall would never have been broken down in the first place. The strongest bulwark of a kingdom, in Henry's reading, is its fidelity to the God who defends it; and the towers Uzziah raised, real and well-placed as they were, would stand or fall with the piety that had prompted them.
10:
Uzziah's care reached beyond the capital into the open country, and the witnesses portray him as a king who loved the land itself. The reformed John Gill sets the towers in the desert of Arabia, built to protect travellers from robbers and, above all, the shepherds and their flocks — buildings, he thinks, like those the Indians call pagodas, not temples but walled enclosures where the herds could be gathered when an alarm was raised. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place these towers in the steppe-lands west of the Dead Sea, the wilderness of Judah so fit for cattle-breeding, raised to guard the herds against the raiding peoples of Edom and Arabia; and they note the many wells he dug to water so much cattle, in the lowland or Shephelah toward the Mediterranean and in the Mishor, the flat tableland east of the Dead Sea — the tribal land of Reuben, which had accordingly at that time come to belong to Judah, as the geography of Deuteronomy 3:10 defines it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott follows the same ground, rendering the desert a grazing country and the "wells" hewn cisterns; the "plain" he too takes as the high level east of Jordan, Reuben's territory, which Uzziah had probably recovered from Moab and Ammon, comparing the claim of the kings of Judah over the eastern country implied at Isaiah 16:1. "Carmel" he reads as the fruitful field or glebe-land of Isaiah 29:17, and glosses the closing verdict, "he loved husbandry," as literally "a lover of the soil was he," recalling the phrase "man of the land" for a husbandman at Genesis 9:20.

Here the schools speak with one warmth. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls the love of husbandry a perfection in a king, for on husbandry every state depends: let commerce be what it may, there can be no true national prosperity if agriculture do not thrive, since even the king himself is served by the field; and where a king encourages tillage, emulation is stirred among his subjects and the earth yields her increase. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds that Uzziah was no lover of war or of sport but delighted in the innocent and quiet employments of the husbandman, and that it is an honour to that calling that one of the most illustrious princes of the house of David followed it and loved it, doubtless overseeing his affairs in the country himself. Wesleyan-arminian John Wesley notes the plainer purpose of the towers — to guard the cattle from the inroads the Arabians were wont to make, and to give notice of the approach of any enemy. The witnesses do not divide: they leave us a portrait of a powerful king who was also a patient farmer, and who found in the soil, no less than on the battlefield, the blessing of the God he was still seeking.
11:
The chapter turns from fields and flocks to the muster-roll, and the witnesses read the notice of Uzziah's standing army as a portrait of ordered military strength. The reformed John Gill states the fact simply: Uzziah had a host of fighting men, a standing army. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch unfold the machinery of it: the host went out to war in bands or detachments, according to the number of their muster made by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer, under the hand of Hananiah, one of the king's captains. The meaning, they explain, is that the mustering by which the army was arranged into its bands was carried out by two officials practised in writing and the keeping of lists, who were placed at the disposal of Hananiah, a prince of the kingdom.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the same picture from the Hebrew. Uzziah, he renders, had "a host doing battle," men who went forth to war "in troops" — in regular array, organised bodies, each house probably forming a distinct troop. "According to the number of their account" he reads as "in the number of their muster," the pequddah or census; and the two royal officials, Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the ruler, he takes to have been entrusted with drafting the muster-rolls, working under the hand — the direction and superintendence — of Hananiah, one of the king's staff officers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the administrative detail into a fuller view of the king's establishment. Uzziah, he observes, seems to have kept up two military bodies: a host of fighting men that went out to war by their bands, whose task was to fetch in spoil from the neighbouring countries by way of reprisal for the raids those nations had so often made upon Judah; and, as the next verses will show, another army for guards and garrisons, ready to defend the country should it be invaded. The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the army, Keil and Ellicott expose the careful census and command that stood behind it, and Henry sets it in the wider frame of a well-ordered war-machine. Behind the bureaucratic language of scribes and musters they let the reader see a kingdom brought to a pitch of organised power — every man numbered, every band captained, the whole force marshalled with a precision that answers to the greatness the chapter has been building, and that will make the coming pride of its master all the more perilous.
12:
The census now gives its totals, and the witnesses pause over the figure of two thousand six hundred heads of fathers' houses. The reformed John Gill takes them for the commanders and principal officers of the army, and reasons that so many officers presuppose a very large host beneath them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the number precisely: the total of the heads of the fathers'-houses, reckoned as valiant heroes, was two thousand six hundred, and subordinate to these — "under their hand" — stood the army of many thousands that the next verse will number. The force, they explain, was thus divided according to the fathers'-houses, so that each house probably formed a single detachment, led by the most valiant among its men; and Keil marks the grammatical nicety, the preposition of subordination that binds the whole army "to the hand" of these chiefs, so that the great host hangs, rank below rank, from the twenty-six hundred names.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the arrangement from the grammar. The "chief of the fathers" are the heads of the families or father-houses; "the mighty men of valour" stands in apposition with them, distinguishing these heads as valiant heroes; and the whole army, he says, was marshalled as of old according to clans, or houses, the chief of each being reckoned among its bravest. It is the ancient tribal order of Israel's host, preserved and set in array under a strong king — the nation organised for war along the very lines of its kinship.

The witnesses do not divide, and the interest of so bare a number lies in what it implies. Gill's inference and Keil's exposition meet on the same point: twenty-six hundred family chiefs are not themselves the army but its framework, the officer-class over a body vastly larger. Ellicott's stress on the clan-structure completes the picture — this is no mercenary levy but the muster of Judah's own households, each ancestral house sending out its band under its own valiant head — the martial order of the nation resting, as it had from the wilderness onward, upon the bonds of kinship. The chronicler, who cares little for the merely military feats of the reign, dwells instead on this careful skeleton of command, and in doing so measures the sheer scale of the power God had given Uzziah while he sought him. The reader is being shown, house by house and captain by captain, just how great this king had grown — the better to feel, when the sixteenth verse arrives, how far there was to fall.
13:
Beneath the twenty-six hundred chiefs stands the full army — three hundred and seven thousand five hundred men — and the witnesses weigh both the number and its purpose. The reformed John Gill observes that this host was larger than the army in his father Amaziah's time by seven thousand five hundred, besides the officers. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe it as an army "that made war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy," and note that Uzziah supplied this whole force with its necessary weapons, the shield, lance, helmet, coat of mail, bows and sling-stones the following verse will list.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the wording and the arithmetic. "An army" he renders an armed force or warlike host, a term found besides only at 1 Chronicles 20:1; and the figure of three hundred thousand, he remarks, fairly agrees with the total of Amaziah's army given at 2 Chronicles 25:5. The phrase "that made war with mighty power" he reads literally as "a doer of battle with strength of might," a sturdy strength; and reckoning the whole against the twenty-six hundred chiefs, he finds each captain set over about a hundred and twenty men, who formed his troop — a division that recalls the familiar "captains of hundreds," though the actual number in each company, as in the Roman army, may have varied. The near-agreement with Amaziah's total, Ellicott implies, is itself a check on the figure: Uzziah did not raise a wholly new army but inherited and enlarged the establishment of his father, the seven thousand five hundred that Gill notes as the increase.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two military establishments into one impression of formidable strength. So great, he says, were the number and the valour of these forces that they made war with mighty power; no enemy durst face them, or at least could not stand before them — for men unarmed can do little in war, and Uzziah had furnished his soldiers with a great armoury. The witnesses do not divide. Gill measures the increase over the previous reign, Keil and Ellicott fix the figure and the command-ratio behind it, and Henry sounds the note of overwhelming might. Yet the chapter's irony hovers even here: all this "mighty power" is the very strength that, unbalanced by humility, will lift up the king's heart. The three hundred thousand who could help him against every earthly enemy could not help him in the one contest that mattered, when he strove not against Philistine or Arab but against his Maker.
14:
The verse turns from the numbering of the army to its equipping, and the witnesses linger over the completeness of the outfit Uzziah provided. The reformed John Gill notes that the king prepared these arms for every soldier throughout the whole host — not a select few but the entire force furnished. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the provision as a strategist's foresight: Uzziah prepared a vast number of military weapons so that he might have them in readiness to put into his subjects' hands upon any sudden emergency.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sorts the armoury into its two classes. Shields, spears — that is, lances — helmets and habergeons, the coats of mail or cuirasses, were for the heavy-armed; and he explains that "habergeon" is an old English word for armour covering neck and breast. The bows and slings were for the light-armed; "slings to cast stones" is literally "stones of slings," and Ellicott judges the phrase mentioned expressly to show that the equipment was complete, down to the very ammunition. Nothing needful for either kind of soldier was wanting: the heavy files armoured at head, breast and body and set with shield and lance, the light skirmishers furnished with bow and sling, and the store replenished with the sling-stones that were their shot. It is the picture of an army outfitted from a royal arsenal rather than left, as older levies often were, to arm itself as best it could.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the observation that binds the list together. Uzziah furnished himself with a great armoury, whence his soldiers were supplied with arms both offensive and defensive — spears, bows and slings for attack, shields, helmets and habergeons for defence. Swords, Henry notes shrewdly, are not mentioned in the catalogue, and probably for the reason that every man already carried a sword of his own, which he wore constantly, so that it needed no special provision from the royal stores. The witnesses do not divide. Gill marks the universality of the equipping, Clarke its prudent forethought, Ellicott its heavy and light divisions, and Henry its offensive and defensive completeness with the telling silence about swords. Between them they show a king who left nothing to chance in the arming of his people — a diligence that was itself, like the towers and the muster, part of the prosperity God gave him while he sought the Lord, and a further measure of the height from which pride would shortly cast him down.
15:
The catalogue of Uzziah's greatness reaches its climax in the war-engines he set upon the walls, and the witnesses treat them as a genuine landmark in the history of warfare. The reformed John Gill likens them to the Roman catapultae, ballistae and scorpiones, and argues from this passage that such machines were not first invented in Greece or Rome but in Judea; drawing on Pliny and Diodorus Siculus, he notes that they were not yet in use when Nineveh was besieged in the days of Sardanapalus, so that the device seems to belong to some skilful men among the Jews in Uzziah's time. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe them as ingenious machines — the Hebrew word meaning things "devised," the invention of cunning artificers — slinging engines answering to the catapults and ballistas of the Romans, by which arrows were shot and great stones propelled from the towers and battlements.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the historic claim furthest. Citing the Targum's picture of ingenious instruments and little hollow towers for shooting arrows and projecting great stones, he calls this the very first intimation on record of any warlike engines for the attack or defence of besieged places, long prior to anything of the kind among Greeks or Romans. Before such inventions, he observes, the besieged could only be starved out, which is why sieges were so tedious: Shalmaneser spent three years before Samaria at 2 Kings 17:5, Sardanapalus held Nineveh seven years, and Troy endured ten — because the besiegers had no engines proper to breach a wall. The Jews alone, Clarke concludes, were the inventors, about eight hundred years before Christ, and no wonder the king's name spread far in consequence. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls this the first mention of artillery, notes that an instrument like the ballista is figured on the Assyrian sculptures, and thinks both kinds of engine passed from Assyria into Palestine.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry alone adds a note of lament amid the wonder: what a pity, he reflects, that the wars and fightings which come from men's lusts should have made it necessary for cunning men to employ their skill in inventing instruments of death. On the fact the witnesses converge — Keil grounding the closing verdict that "his name spread far abroad, for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong." That last clause, all of them feel, is the hinge of the chapter. The marvellous help had brought him to strength; and it is at the summit of that strength, with his engines on the towers and his fame at the gates of Egypt, that the next verse will turn the whole story over. Henry's sigh over the instruments of death is answered by the deeper irony to come, that the king so marvellously helped would presently lift up the helped hand against the God who helped it.
16:
"But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction" — and the witnesses read this verse as the tragic hinge on which the whole reign turns. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark how the very strength that God had given became the occasion of ruin: with a lofty feeling of his power, Uzziah wished to make himself the high priest of his own kingdom, as the kings of Egypt and of other nations were at once monarchs and supreme pontiffs, and to unite all sacred and civil power in his single person. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same ambition, rendering "to his destruction" more literally "even to dealing corruptly," and "he transgressed" as "he was unfaithful to Jehovah" in the sense of 1 Chronicles 5:25. Elevated by success, Uzziah desired to become supreme pontiff as well as king, like the Egyptian Pharaohs; and Ellicott weighs, only to doubt, the notion that he merely revived a precedent of David and Solomon, for it can hardly be proved that those monarchs, organisers of the ritual though they were, ever performed the distinctive functions of priests — and he sets the act beside the presumption of Saul at 1 Samuel 13:9 and its consequences.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes this the only blot on Uzziah's name, and traces it to its root. That which was at the bottom of his sin, he says, was pride of heart, a lust that ruins more than any other: when he was strong, and marvellously helped by God till he was so, instead of lifting up the name of God in gratitude, his heart was lifted up to his destruction — for thus the prosperity of fools, by puffing them up with pride, destroys them. Henry notes how his sin differed from his predecessors': theirs was forsaking the temple of the Lord to burn incense on idolatrous altars, his was intruding into the temple further than was allowed, attempting to burn incense on the altar of God. See, he warns, how hard it is to avoid one extreme and not run into another.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fix the offence in the law. Adam Clarke says the king assumed to himself the priest's office, and refers the whole transaction to his notes on 2 Kings 15:5; John Wesley specifies that he went into the holy place where the altar of incense stood, into which none but the priests might enter, much less offer incense. Ellicott grounds the prohibition in the law of Numbers 18:1-7. The witnesses do not divide: whether they call it pride, corruption, or unfaithfulness, all agree that the strength which was God's gift became, uncrowned by humility, the very engine of the king's fall — and Henry adds the gospel note, that the incense of our prayers must by faith be put into the hands of our Lord Jesus, the great High Priest of our profession, or it cannot be accepted, as Revelation 8:3 teaches.
17:
Against the king's presumption the witnesses set the courage of the priesthood, as Azariah and his company move to bar the way. The reformed John Gill notes that Azariah the priest went in after Uzziah to hinder him from the act and to persuade him to withdraw, and identifies him as the high priest, thought to be the same named in the earlier genealogy. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out the confrontation: the king's purpose was opposed by the high priest Azariah and eighty priests of the Lord, valiant men who had the courage to represent to him that to burn incense to the Lord did not appertain to the king but only to the sanctified sons of Aaron. Azariah, they add, is styled the chief priest, and is in all probability the high priest mentioned at 1 Chronicles 6:10.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the office and weighs the striking epithet. Azariah is the high priest, whose proper duty it would be to resist such an encroachment upon the sacerdotal functions; and the eighty priests are called "valiant men," literally "sons of valour," so named, Ellicott suggests, not for any feat of arms but because they had the moral courage to oppose the king to his face. It is a courage of conscience, not of the sword: eighty men of God standing unarmed before an angry and powerful monarch, armed only with the law they were sworn to guard.

The witnesses do not divide, and the scene they describe is a rare and telling one. Here is no prophet denouncing from a distance but the ordained ministry itself, the high priest at its head, physically interposing between the king and the altar he means to profane. Gill marks their aim — to hinder and to persuade; Keil and Ellicott mark their courage and their argument — that the priesthood belongs to Aaron's consecrated line and to no one else, however exalted. The chronicler, who has spent the chapter magnifying Uzziah's strength, now shows that strength met and checked by a higher authority than any army: the plain word of God's law, spoken by men willing to risk a king's wrath to uphold it. The stage is set for the collision of the two powers, royal and priestly, that the law of Moses had deliberately kept apart — and the next verses will show which of them the God of Israel vindicates.
18:
The priests' remonstrance is now given in full, and the witnesses read it as a firm but reverent rebuke. The reformed John Gill catches the physical force of the verb: they not only stood against Uzziah but stood about him, surrounding him so as to hinder his approach to the altar of incense. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the phrase "withstood" as a late Hebrew usage, and unfolds their words: "It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated" — "trespassed" being the same word "dealt faithlessly" of the sixteenth verse. The closing clause, "neither shall it be for thine honour from the Lord God," Ellicott renders, "thine act will not issue in honour, as thou thinkest, but in shame."

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the manner of the opposition with care. "Withstood" is, in the Hebrew, "stood up against" Uzziah — yet not by force or by laying hands upon him to restrain him, for in the very next verse the censer is still found in his hand, but only by admonition and reproof. Their warning, "neither shall it be for thine honour," Wesley paraphrases: expect rather that God will punish thee, or put some brand of infamy upon thee, for this presumption. And he adds the fine observation that the priests expressed even this modestly, because they considered that the man to whom they spoke, offender though he was, was still their sovereign.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the narrative forward through the whole crisis, from the priests' resistance to the sudden breaking out of the leprosy and the king's expulsion. But the weight of this verse the witnesses lay on the words themselves. The priests advance no opinion of their own; they cite the settled ordinance of the law — incense belongs to the consecrated sons of Aaron and to none beside. Gill fixes their bodily interposition, Ellicott the exactness of their legal charge, Wesley the reverent restraint with which even a rebuked king is still honoured as king. The witnesses do not divide. They show a confrontation conducted wholly within the bounds of God's word: no violence, no faction, only the plain law urged plainly, and a solemn forewarning that to press on will bring not honour but disgrace — a warning the next verse will see fulfilled upon the king's own forehead in the instant of his rage.
19:
The king's fury and its instant punishment fill this verse, and the witnesses read the leprosy as a stroke from heaven answering to the sin. The reformed John Gill records that Uzziah was wroth with the priests and, as Josephus reports, even threatened to kill them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the anger vividly — the word means to foam with rage — and notes the censer already in his hand, as at Ezekiel 8:11; the leprosy "rose up," a verb used in this sense nowhere else, and broke out "from beside," that is hard by, the altar. Uzziah's punishment, Ellicott observes, was the very same that fell upon Miriam at Numbers 12:10 and upon Gehazi at 2 Kings 5:27. He records too the embellishments of Josephus — that the great earthquake named at Amos 1:1 struck at the moment the king threatened the priests, and that a ray of sunlight, falling through the temple roof cloven by the shock, produced the leprosy, a tradition he links to the shaking foretold at Zechariah 14:5.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the stroke as unmistakably divine: the leprosy appeared in his forehead so that he could not hide his shame, though probably it seized the rest of his body too; and it came "from beside" the altar by a blow from an invisible hand, that the king might be assured this was the direct effect of God's displeasure. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the moment in its moral logic: had Uzziah submitted to the priests' admonition and gone back, all would have been well; but when he was wroth with them and would not part with the censer, then God was wroth with him and smote him — for if presumptuous men will not be made to see their error by the judgments of God's mouth, they shall be made to see it by the judgments of his hand.

One dissenting note reaches the witnesses. Ellicott reports the critic Thenius, who, while granting the historical reality of Uzziah's invasion of the sanctuary, held that the chronicler merely followed traditional exegesis in construing the king's leprosy as a judgment upon his offence. But Ellicott answers that the chronicler has given the story as he found it in the history of Uzziah to which he alludes at 2 Chronicles 26:22, and all the other witnesses stand with him: the disease is no pious construction but the very hand of God, falling on the forehead the king had lifted up in pride, in the instant of his rage, before the altar he had dared to usurp.
20:
The priests turn and see the mark of God upon the king, and the witnesses follow the swift, dreadful reversal. The reformed John Gill observes that Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked upon Uzziah and beheld him leprous in his forehead: he was no doubt leprous over his whole body, but it appeared there most remarkably, seen by them all, who without doubt informed him of his case, of which he soon became sensible. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the Hebrew: they "turned towards him" and, seeing the leprosy, "thrust him out," the verb meaning they scared or hurried him from the place, as at Esther 6:14; and "he hasted also" is literally "he thrust himself," a late word occurring thrice in Esther and not elsewhere. The reason given, that the Lord had smitten him, Ellicott ties to the parallel account of the affliction at 2 Kings 15:5.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks how little compulsion was needed. "Thrust" here is not by force, which was not required, for the king voluntarily hasted away; the priests urged him out by vehement persuasions and by denunciations of God's further judgments should he refuse to depart. The panic and the flight are the king's own; the ministers have only to speak, and the leprous monarch, who a moment before would not surrender the censer, now cannot get out of the sanctuary fast enough.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the meaning of that flight. When the leprosy appeared, he says, the priests were emboldened to thrust him out; nay, he himself hasted to go out, because the Lord had smitten him with a disease that was in a special manner the token of his displeasure, and that he knew secluded him from all common converse with men, much more from the altar of God. Here Henry finds a flicker of grace even in judgment: it evinced some religious fear of God in the king's heart that, as soon as he found God was angry, he not only let fall his attempt but retired with the utmost precipitation — for though he strove with the priests, he would not strive with his Maker. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the forehead where the plague showed, Ellicott the hurried expulsion and the smiting hand, Wesley the persuasion that needed no force, and Henry the king's own terror and the fear of God still stirring beneath it. The proud intruder is driven from the house he meant to command, and goes willingly, because the God he had defied has set a visible seal of exclusion upon his brow.
21:
The stroke that fell in an instant becomes the settled condition of the rest of the king's life, and the witnesses read the sentence with its full severity. The reformed John Gill notes only that Uzziah was a leper unto the day of his death and dwelt in a separate house, referring the reader to his fuller treatment of the parallel. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the isolation: he dwelt in a several house, separated because of the infectious nature of his disorder from all society — domestic, civil, and religious — while his son Jotham became regent of the land, his father being no longer able to perform the functions of the regal office.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the "several house" more exactly as a hospital or lazar-house, and dwells on the clause the chronicler alone adds — "for he was cut off from the house of the Lord." Having been formally excluded as a leper from the sacred precincts, Ellicott explains, Uzziah was obliged to isolate himself from society altogether, in obedience to the law of the leper at Leviticus 13:46; and the phrase "cut off" he compares with the language of desolation at Psalms 88:5.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the awful fitness of it all. God would have this leprosy be incurable, he says, as a lasting monument of his anger against such presumptuous invaders of the priest's office; and Uzziah dwelt apart as the law obliged him, daring not now to resist, being under the hand of God and in fear of worse plagues. Then Wesley draws the correspondence the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had also seen: the punishment answered the sin as face answers to face in a glass. He thrust himself into the temple of God, whither the priests only had admission, and for that he is thrust out of the very courts of the temple into which the meanest of his subjects might freely enter; he invaded the dignity of the priesthood, to which he had no right, and for that he is deprived even of the royal dignity, to which he had an undoubted right. Henry adds that while the king was a leper he was as good as dead — dead while he lived, and buried alive — so that the law was in effect answered which said the stranger that came nigh should be put to death; and the disgrace survived him, for when he died they would not bury him among the kings. The witnesses do not divide: they leave a monarch stripped of throne and temple alike, shut in his lazar-house, a living parable that those who covet forbidden honours forfeit the honours that were lawfully their own.
22:
The chronicler closes the reign with his customary reference to the sources, and the witnesses attend both to the record and to its loss. The reformed John Gill notes that the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, were written down — all that he did, from the beginning of his reign to its end. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch state the fact plainly: the history of his reign was written by the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz, and refer the reader to their Introduction for the bearing of this on the composition of the book.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on what is missing. This work of Isaiah's, he observes, is totally lost; for we have no history of this king in the writings of the prophet that survive to us — Uzziah is barely mentioned in the book of Isaiah, only at Isaiah 1:1 in the heading and at Isaiah 6:1, where the prophet dates his great vision to the year of the king's death. Whatever fuller chronicle Isaiah once composed of Uzziah's acts has perished, leaving only the epitome the chronicler drew from it. That the reign's own historian should have been the prophet whose ministry it dates — whose call, Gill and Clarke both recall, is fixed to the year of this king's death — binds the throne and the prophetic word together at the very seam of the record.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the attribution — "did Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, write" — and marks the divergence from the parallel: where Chronicles names the prophet's own composition, the book of Kings refers instead to "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the scope of the record, first and last; Keil and Ellicott the authorship; Clarke the melancholy fact that so great a prophet's history of so great a king has not come down to us. Between them they remind the reader that the inspired narrative before us is a distillation, chosen and shaped from a fuller account now beyond recovery — and that the one thing the Spirit has preserved of this long and mighty reign is not the catalogue of its conquests but the lesson of its pride, the towering strength and the leprous fall. What the chronicler has kept is precisely what the church most needed to keep: not the annals of Uzziah's greatness, but the warning of his end.
23:
The reign ends as it was bound to end, with a burial that carries the leprosy's stigma to the grave, and the witnesses read the last verse as a final seal upon the judgment. The reformed John Gill notes that Uzziah slept with his fathers, dying, on Lightfoot's reckoning, in the very year he had been smitten with the leprosy; and it was in the year of his death, Gill recalls, that Isaiah was granted the great temple vision recorded at Isaiah 6:1. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the manner of the burial: because Uzziah had died a leper, he was not laid in the graves of the kings themselves but only in their neighbourhood, in the burial-field that belonged to the kings, that his body might not defile the royal sepulchres.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same exclusion. As a leper, he was not permitted to be buried in the common burying-place of the kings, since it was supposed that even a place of sepulture might be defiled by the body of one who had died of so afflictive and dangerous a malady. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms and refines it: they buried him in the burial-field or graveyard belonging to the kings, and near their tombs, but not in the royal sepulchres themselves, because a leper would have polluted them — whereas the parallel at 2 Kings 15:7 says only, as usual, that he was buried "in the city of David."

The witnesses do not divide, and the pathos of their agreement is plain. A king who had ruled two-and-fifty years, whose name had reached the border of Egypt, who had subdued Philistines and Ammonites and armed a host of three hundred thousand, is carried at last to a field beside the tombs of his fathers, refused a place among them lest his very corpse defile the royal dust. The exclusion that had shut him from the temple and the throne in life follows him into death: buried apart, remembered as a leper. Yet the chronicler does not close in unrelieved gloom, and Gill's quiet detail lets a further light fall — that the year which laid this proud king in his separate grave was the year the young Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, and heard the seraphim cry Holy. The earthly throne is emptied and its occupant disgraced; and in that same year the prophet is shown the throne that does not empty, and the King whose glory fills the house Uzziah had dared to profane. So the record of a reign begun in piety and ruined by pride ends not merely in a leper's grave but on the threshold of a greater vision, a mortal king laid low that the eternal King might be seen.
2:
The single notice that Uzziah "built Eloth, and restored it to Judah" the witnesses read as the young king's first and characteristic act, a stroke that completed his father's unfinished work at the head of the Red Sea. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as the head of the whole record of Uzziah's wars and buildings: at the very outset of his reign, they explain, he completed the subjection of the Edomites which his father Amaziah had begun, by capturing and fortifying the seaport of Elath — and it is from this recovered harbour that his later campaigns against Philistia and Arabia will proceed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps his comment brief, noting that this is the port whose history he had already traced at 2 Kings 14:21, and reminding the reader that the king is called by several different names, as he had shown at 2 Kings 15:1.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the emphatic Hebrew, "it was he who built" Eloth — the pronoun throwing the whole weight of the achievement on Uzziah personally. Eloth, he notes, is the Elath of the Kings account, the Idumean port on the Red Sea, the strategic outlet toward the trade of the south and the key to any dominion over Edom; and he observes that these opening verses of the chapter stand identical, almost word for word, with the parallel in Kings, so that the reader is to consult the notes there for the accession, the mother's name, and the general verdict on the reign.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott alike see in the rebuilding of Elath the mark of a vigorous and far-sighted prince, one who at sixteen already grasped that the road to Judah's greatness ran through the mastery of Edom and the sea. Clarke and Ellicott secure the identity of the harbour and the seam where the chronicler takes over his older source unchanged. Between them they show the reign beginning as it will for a long time continue — in energetic, God-helped success, the recovery of a lost possession and the extension of the kingdom's reach, all set down as the fruit of the piety the previous verse had named. The dry building-notice is thus the first instance of the principle that while Uzziah sought the Lord, God made him to prosper; the leprosy that will close the chapter is still far off, and here all is promise.
